“Epiphysis = Giant cell; Metaphysis = Osteosarcoma; Diaphysis = Ewing.”

Bone tumour basics Basics

  • Primary (bone-forming, cartilage-forming, unknown origin) vs secondary (metastases, far more common).
  • Benign lesions: common, often incidental, mostly in the first three decades. In older adults a bone tumour is more likely malignant.
  • Presentation: pain, slow-growing mass, or pathologic fracture.
BONE-FORMING

Osteoid osteoma Benign

Spot it: Night pain relieved by aspirin.
  • Young men; cortex of femur/tibia; <2 cm.
  • Thick reactive cortical rim may be the only X-ray clue.
  • Severe night pain relieved by aspirin/NSAIDs (PGE2 from osteoblasts; NSAIDs block COX).
  • Gross: round-to-oval hemorrhagic gritty tan mass. Micro: well circumscribed, woven-bone trabeculae rimmed by osteoblasts, loose stroma, congested capillaries.

Osteoblastoma Benign

Spot it: Large vertebral lesion, no aspirin response.
  • Young adults; posterior vertebral elements; >2 cm.
  • Little reactive bone; pain not relieved by aspirin.
  • Histology resembles osteoid osteoma but differs clinically and radiographically.

Osteosarcoma Malignant

Spot it: Malignant cells producing osteoid.
  • Most common primary malignant bone tumour; malignant cells make osteoid/bone (diagnostic).
  • Bimodal: 75% <20 y; second peak in older adults (Paget disease, bone infarcts, radiation).
  • Metaphysis of distal femur/proximal tibia.
  • X-ray: large destructive mixed lytic + sclerotic mass, infiltrative margins, Codman triangle (raised periosteum; not pathognomonic).
  • Gross: bulky gritty gray-white, hemorrhage, cystic degeneration. Micro: pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei, giant cells, vascular invasion, many mitoses.
  • Aggressive; lung metastasis. Neoadjuvant chemo → surgery → chemo; % necrosis after chemo = prognosis.
CARTILAGE-FORMING

Osteochondroma Benign

Spot it: Cartilage-capped bony projection continuous with bone.
  • Exostosis: cartilage-capped bony outgrowth attached by a stalk.
  • Solitary: late adolescence/early adulthood; multiple (hereditary exostoses): childhood.
  • Metaphysis near growth plate, especially the knee; slow-growing mass.
  • Sessile or pedunculated, 1–20 cm; hyaline cartilage cap + perichondrium; cortex continuous with host bone.

Enchondroma Benign

  • Benign hyaline cartilage tumour inside the bone (medulla); 20–50 y; small bones of hands/feet.
  • Mostly asymptomatic; may cause pain or pathologic fracture.
  • X-ray: circumscribed lucency, central calcification, sclerotic rim, intact cortex. Gross: <3 cm, gray-blue, translucent.
  • Ollier disease / Maffucci syndrome: multiple enchondromas (enchondromatosis), higher malignant risk, digit deformities.

Chondrosarcoma Malignant

Spot it: Malignant cartilage trapping bone trabeculae.
  • Malignant cartilage-producing tumour; half as common as osteosarcoma.
  • Conventional (90%, age 40+), dedifferentiated (old), clear cell and mesenchymal (young).
  • Axial skeleton: pelvis, shoulder, ribs; ~15% secondary to enchondroma/osteochondroma.
  • Gross: bulky glistening gray-white cartilage nodules with myxoid areas, necrosis, cysts; breaks cortex into soft tissue.
  • Micro: malignant cartilage infiltrates marrow and entraps trabeculae; grade 1–3 (cellularity, atypia, mitoses).
  • Grade 3: 70% spread to lungs; treated by wide excision (+ chemo for dedifferentiated/mesenchymal).
OTHER BONE TUMOURS

Ewing sarcoma Malignant

Spot it: Child + diaphysis + small round blue cells.
  • Primitive small round cells with neuroectodermal features; 2nd most common childhood bone sarcoma.
  • Diaphysis of long bones (can be extraskeletal); painful, warm, swollen mass.
  • t(11;22) EWSR1–FLI1 fusion gene (balanced translocation).
  • X-ray: permeative lytic lesion, onion-skin and sunburst periosteal reaction.
  • Micro: sheets of small round blue cells, Homer-Wright rosettes.
  • Neoadjuvant chemo → surgery ± radiation.

Giant cell tumour Locally aggressive

Spot it: Adult epiphyseal lesion with many giant cells.
  • Adults; epiphysis of distal femur/proximal tibia (near joints → arthritis-like pain, fractures).
  • X-ray: radiolucent, destroys cortex, thin shell of reactive bone. Gross: red-brown with cystic change.
  • Micro: osteoclast-type giant cells (100+ nuclei) among mononuclear stromal cells (the true neoplastic cells).
  • Curettage; 40–60% recur, ≤4% lung metastases.

Bone metastases Secondary

  • Far outnumber primary bone cancers; poor prognosis (advanced disease).
  • Adults: prostate, breast, kidney, lung. Children: neuroblastoma, Wilms tumour, rhabdomyosarcoma.
  • Multifocal, axial skeleton/vertebrae. Spread: direct, lymphatic, hematogenous, intraspinal seeding.
  • Lytic (RANKL ↑ osteoclasts), blastic (WNT ↑ osteoblasts) or mixed.
SOFT TISSUE TUMOURS (fat, muscle, fibrous tissue)

Lipoma Benign

  • Most common adult soft tissue tumour.
  • Subcutis of proximal limbs/trunk, middle age.
  • Well-encapsulated mature adipocytes; cured by simple excision.

Liposarcoma Malignant

  • Adults 50s–60s; deep soft tissue and retroperitoneum (grows large before symptoms); recurs locally unless widely excised.
  • Well-differentiated: adipocytes + atypical spindle cells; MDM2 amplification; indolent.
  • Myxoid: primitive lipoblasts in basophilic myxoid matrix; t(12;16); intermediate.
  • Pleomorphic: anaplastic cells + lipoblasts; complex karyotype; aggressive, metastasizes.

Nodular fasciitis Benign

  • Self-limited fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation; young adults, upper limb.
  • Rapid growth over weeks after trauma (rapid growth ≠ malignant).
  • Micro: plump immature fibroblasts in a tissue-culture-like pattern, many mitoses, lymphocytes, extravasated RBCs.
  • May regress; rarely recurs; no malignant transformation.
